rules.message: Combining retinol with glycolic acid may increase irritation. Many dermatology sources suggest alternating nights (glycolic acid one evening, retinol another) rather than applying both at once.
rules.reason: Both retinol and glycolic acid (an AHA) can irritate skin on their own; layering them increases that risk for many users.

rules.message: Combining retinol with salicylic acid can be drying. A commonly cited approach is using salicylic acid in the morning and retinol at night rather than layering them.
rules.reason: Both retinol and salicylic acid (a BHA) can dry out skin; using them at the same time compounds that effect for many users.

rules.message: Retinoid + benzoyl peroxide is a recognized, commonly prescribed combination (sold together in products like Epiduo), not something to avoid -- but documented possible side effects of this combination include dryness, irritated skin, peeling, and burning.
rules.reason: This is a widely used, FDA-recognized combination for acne treatment, but it carries a documented irritation profile worth being aware of.

rules.message: It's commonly recommended to use a vitamin C product in the morning and retinol at night, rather than layering them in the same routine step.
rules.reason: This is a routine-sequencing recommendation, not a documented safety concern -- the two are not described as unsafe to combine.

rules.message: Niacinamide is commonly cited as a complementary pairing with retinol -- it may help offset some of the irritation retinol can cause for certain users, rather than conflicting with it.
rules.reason: Niacinamide is noted for skin-protective, soothing effects that may counteract retinol-related irritation.

rules.message: Hyaluronic acid is commonly used alongside retinol to help offset dryness, not because of any conflict between the two ingredients.
rules.reason: Hyaluronic acid functions as a hydrating humectant that may counteract retinol-related dryness.
